blocks.text: First, the Writing Trap Library: the mistakes that most often cap a Writing score, gathered in one place for revision. Then the time plan that gives each task its proper share of the hour.
PART 12
THE WRITING TRAP LIBRARY

Several of these traps appeared across the module. Here they are consolidated, each with what it looks like, why students fall for it, how to recognise it, how to avoid it, and an example. Traps 9 to 11 are Task 1 specific; the rest are mainly Task 2.
Trap 1: Answering only part of the question

Looks like: the prompt has two or three parts, and the essay covers only one or two. Why students fall: they answer the part they find easiest and forget the rest. Recognise it: count the tasks in the prompt (File 19); if your essay has fewer parts, you have fallen in. Avoid it: write the number of tasks in the margin and give each a paragraph. Example: “Discuss both views and give your opinion,” answered with both views but no opinion. Task Response capped. (See Files 16, 19.)
Trap 2: Unclear position

Looks like: an opinion essay where the reader cannot tell what the writer actually thinks. Why students fall: they present both sides to seem balanced, and never commit. Recognise it: if a reader could not state your position in one sentence, it is unclear. Avoid it: state your position in the introduction and hold it consistently to the conclusion. Example: an “agree or disagree” essay that argues both sides equally. (See File 19.)
Trap 3: Too many ideas

Looks like: an essay listing five or six points, none developed. Why students fall: they believe more ideas mean a higher score. Recognise it: your body paragraphs each contain several undeveloped points. Avoid it: choose two or three ideas and develop each fully. Example: a body paragraph naming five reasons in five sentences, explaining none. (See File 20.)
Trap 4: Undeveloped ideas

Looks like: points that are stated but never explained or illustrated. Why students fall: they skip the explanation and example steps. Recognise it: your paragraphs are short and read as assertions. Avoid it: use Point, Explanation, Example, Consequence on every main idea. Example: “Pollution is bad for health. Governments should act.” No reasoning, no example. (See File 20.)
Trap 5: Irrelevant examples

Looks like: an example that does not actually support the point, or wanders off topic. Why students fall: they reach for any example rather than a fitting one, or force an off-topic idea. Recognise it: the example does not clearly illustrate the sentence before it. Avoid it: choose examples that directly demonstrate the point; drop forced ones (File 19). Example: arguing that online shopping harms high streets, then giving an example about computer electricity use. (See File 19.)
Trap 6: Memorised essays and phrases

Looks like: chunks of pre-learned text that could fit any prompt. Why students fall: they hope a memorised structure or phrase will save effort. Recognise it: phrases like “since the dawn of time” or a body that does not quite fit the question. Avoid it: write about the specific question in your own words. Example: “In this fast-paced modern world, it is a double-edged sword.” Discounted on sight. (See File 21.)
Trap 7: Generic introductions

Looks like: an introduction that copies the prompt or says nothing specific. Why students fall: they do not know how to open, so they restate the question. Recognise it: your introduction contains the prompt's exact words, or no position. Avoid it: paraphrase the topic in your own words and state your position or outline. Example: copying “Some people think that… while others believe…” verbatim. Scores nothing for Lexical Resource. (See Files 16, 20.)
Trap 8: Repetitive conclusions

Looks like: a conclusion that repeats the introduction word for word, or adds a new idea. Why students fall: they run out of time or ideas and either copy or improvise. Recognise it: your conclusion either mirrors the intro exactly or raises something new. Avoid it: restate the position and summarise the reasons in fresh words; add nothing new. Example: a conclusion introducing a brand-new argument in its final sentence. (See File 20.)
Trap 9: Data dumping (Task 1)

Looks like: every number in the visual reported in order, with no shape. Why students fall: they think completeness is rewarded. Recognise it: your Task 1 answer is a list of figures. Avoid it: select significant data, group it, and compare (File 18). Example: “Cinema was 140, then 135, then 125…” (See File 18.)
Trap 10: No clear overview (Task 1)

Looks like: a Task 1 answer with no summary of the main features. Why students fall: they start describing detail immediately and forget the overview. Recognise it: there is no “Overall” sentence capturing the big picture. Avoid it: write the overview straight after the introduction, with no numbers. Example: a Task 1 answer that jumps into figures with no big-picture sentence. Caps the score. (See File 18.)
Trap 11: Poor grouping (Task 1)

Looks like: each category described separately, with no comparison. Why students fall: they take the categories one at a time as listed. Recognise it: your paragraphs describe items in isolation. Avoid it: group categories that behave alike and contrast them. Example: three flat sentences (“Cinema fell. DVDs fell. Streaming rose.”) instead of one grouped contrast. (See File 18.)
Trap 12: Overusing linking words

Looks like: a connector at the start of almost every sentence. Why students fall: they were taught that more linkers mean better cohesion. Recognise it: “Firstly, Moreover, Furthermore, In addition” open your sentences in sequence. Avoid it: connect through logic and referencing; use linkers only where the logic turns. Example: “Firstly… Moreover… Furthermore… In addition…” (See File 21.)

blocks.title: TUTOR INSIDER TIP
blocks.text: The most expensive traps are the ones decided before you write: answering the wrong question, missing a part, and having no clear position. These cap your Task Response no matter how well you write. Spend the first minute on task analysis, and you remove the three costliest traps at a stroke.
blocks.bn: সবচেয়ে ব্যয়বহুল ফাঁদগুলো লেখার আগেই ধরা হয়: ভুল প্রশ্নের উত্তর, একটা অংশ বাদ, আর অস্পষ্ট অবস্থান। এগুলো যতই ভালোই লিখুন Task Response আটকে দেয়। প্রথম মিনিটটা task analysis-এ দিন।

blocks.text: PART 13
THE 60-MINUTE WRITING PLAN
The split, and why Task 2 gets more
Sixty minutes, two tasks. The recommended split is about twenty minutes for Task 1 and forty for Task 2.

Task 2 is worth roughly twice as much as Task 1 in your Writing score, so it deserves roughly twice the time. The most common and costly timing error is polishing Task 1 while Task 2 goes unfinished. Never sacrifice the more valuable task for the less valuable one.
Task 1: twenty minutes

items: Read and plan (3 to 4 minutes): identify the visual type, read the frame and units, find the main features and the overview, decide what to select. (Files 17, 18.)
Write (about 14 minutes): introduction, overview, one or two body paragraphs of selected, grouped, compared data. Aim comfortably above 150 words.
Check (about 2 minutes): overview present, main features covered, no data dump, word count met.

blocks.text: Task 2: forty minutes

items: Analyse and plan (about 5 minutes): identify the type, decide your position, generate ideas with the lens menu, and sketch a paragraph plan. (Files 16, 19.)
Write (about 30 minutes): introduction with position, two or three developed body paragraphs, conclusion. Aim comfortably above 250 words.
Check (about 5 minutes): every part of the question answered, position clear, ideas developed, no memorised phrases, no new idea in the conclusion. (File 23.)

blocks.text: Which task first?
Both orders work, and you should choose based on your own tendency.
Task 1 first is the common choice: it is shorter and acts as a warm-up before the heavier essay.

Task 2 first is the safer choice if you tend to run out of time, because it protects the more valuable task. Write Task 2 while you are fresh and the clock is generous, then do Task 1 in the time that remains.
The rule behind both: whichever you do first, guard Task 2's time. If you are the kind of candidate who over-invests in Task 1, do Task 2 first and remove the temptation.
Planning is not wasted time

Five minutes of planning on Task 2 feels like time not writing, but it prevents the most expensive errors: the wrong structure, the missing part, the blank mind halfway through. A planned essay is faster to write and far less likely to fall into the traps above. The candidates who skip planning are usually the ones who run out of both ideas and time.
Word-count discipline

Do not undershoot: writing below 150 or 250 words is penalised. Do not massively overshoot either: a very long essay wastes time you need for checking and usually contains more errors. Aim a little above the minimum, then stop and check.

blocks.title: TUTOR INSIDER TIP
blocks.text: If you must leave one task slightly unfinished, it should never be Task 2. A complete Task 2 and a slightly short Task 1 will almost always score higher than a perfect Task 1 and a rushed, incomplete Task 2. Protect the bigger task with your life.
blocks.bn: যদি একটা টাস্ক কিছুটা অসম্পূর্ণ রাখতেই হয়, সেটা কখনো Task 2 নয়। সম্পূর্ণ Task 2 আর একটা ছোটো Task 1 প্রায় সবসময় নিখুঁত Task 1 আর তাড়াহুডো অসম্পূর্ণ Task 2-এর চেয়ে বেশি নম্বর পায়।

blocks.text: PRACTICE
Reasoning keys follow.

blocks.label: Drill 22.1 (Level 2): Name the trap
blocks.prompt:
1. A Task 1 answer with no “Overall” sentence.
2. An essay whose conclusion introduces a new argument.
3. An opinion essay arguing both sides equally.
4. A body paragraph listing six reasons, none explained.
blocks.answer:
1. No clear overview (Trap 10). The single most damaging Task 1 omission.
2. Repetitive conclusion / new idea in conclusion (Trap 8). A conclusion must not open new arguments.
3. Unclear position (Trap 2). An opinion essay must commit.
4. Too many ideas plus undeveloped ideas (Traps 3 and 4). Depth, not a longer list, is needed.

blocks.label: Drill 22.2 (Level 2): Fix the timing
blocks.prompt: A candidate spends 32 minutes on Task 1 and 25 minutes on Task 2, leaving Task 2 unfinished. What went wrong, and what should they do next time?
blocks.answer: The candidate inverted the time split, giving the shorter, less valuable task more time than the longer, more valuable one, and sacrificed Task 2, which is worth double. Next time: cap Task 1 at twenty minutes and move on even if it is not perfect, or do Task 2 first to protect it. A finished Task 2 matters far more than a flawless Task 1.

blocks.label: Drill 22.3 (Level 3): Plan the hour
blocks.prompt: You have a Task 1 line graph and a Task 2 discussion essay. Sketch how you would spend the 60 minutes, including planning and checking, and say which you would do first and why.
blocks.answer:
Task 1 first (a line graph is quick to plan): 3 to 4 minutes reading and finding the overview, about 14 minutes writing, 2 minutes checking. Then Task 2: about 5 minutes analysing the discussion prompt and planning both views plus my opinion with the lens menu, about 30 minutes writing, 5 minutes checking. I would do Task 1 first here because a line graph is straightforward and warms me up, but I would watch the clock and stop Task 1 at twenty minutes no matter what, to protect Task 2's forty. If I knew I tended to overrun on Task 1, I would do Task 2 first instead.
The lesson: the plan is not rigid, but the priority is: Task 2 gets its full share, planning and checking are built in, and Task 1 is capped so it cannot steal the essay's time.

blocks.text: The final Writing chapter. First, how to check your work in the last few minutes so you recover marks instead of wasting the time. Then a progressive set of practice drills that pull the whole module together, ending with a timed challenge and a band comparison that shows you exactly what lifts an essay.
PART 14
SELF-CHECKING
Check strategically, not randomly

You will have a few minutes at the end of each task, and they are valuable, but only if you spend them on the right things. Random re-reading finds little. A priority checklist finds the biggest, most recoverable losses first.

Self-checking is not line-by-line grammar proofreading. Grammar has its own book in this series, and a deep grammar audit is neither possible nor most valuable in three minutes. Check in priority order, highest-impact first: did you answer the question, is your position clear, is it organised and relevant. These recover far more marks than hunting for a missing article.
The checklist, in priority order
Run these in order. Stop worrying about the low ones if the high ones are not right.

items: Task completion. Did you answer every part of the question? For Task 1, is there an overview and are the main features covered? This is the highest-impact check, because a missing part or overview caps your score.
Position (Task 2). Is your opinion clear and consistent from introduction to conclusion? Could a reader state it in one sentence?
Organisation. One idea per paragraph, clear paragraph breaks, logical order? Can you name each paragraph's job?
Relevance. Does every paragraph actually answer the question? Is there an off-topic sentence or forced example to cut?
Repetition. Any word or idea repeated so often it should be varied or removed?
Obvious errors. Glaring spelling mistakes, missing words, or clearly wrong words, the ones that jump out on a read-through. Not a deep grammar hunt; the surface errors a reader would notice.
Word count. Did you meet the minimum comfortably?

blocks.text: How to do it in three to five minutes

Two quick passes. First pass, read for content: task completion, position, relevance. This is where the marks are. Second pass, read for surface: obvious spelling and missing words. Fix what you can quickly and cleanly.
Do not over-edit

Under time pressure, do not rewrite whole sentences or restructure paragraphs; you risk introducing new errors and leaving a mess half-finished. Make small, safe corrections. If a sentence is understandable, leave it. The check is for catching clear problems, not for perfecting prose you have no time to perfect.

blocks.title: TUTOR INSIDER TIP
blocks.text: Spend your first check on content, not commas. A misplaced comma costs almost nothing; a missing half of the question costs a whole band. Read first to confirm you answered everything asked, and only then look at surface errors. Most candidates check in exactly the wrong order and fix trivia while a capped Task Response sits untouched.
blocks.bn: প্রথম check-টা content-এ দিন, কমায় নয়। ভাল কমা প্রায় কিছুই কারে না; প্রশ্নের অর্ধেক বাদ পড়লে পুরো একটা band নষ্ট হয়। আগে নিশ্চিত করুন সব উত্তর দিয়েছেন, তারপর ছোট ভুল দেখুন।

blocks.text: PART 15
WRITING PRACTICE
Progressive drills that assemble the module. Guidance keys follow each group.
Analysis and idea drills

blocks.label: Drill 23.1 (question analysis)
blocks.prompt: For each, name the type and what to deliver. a) “Some think advertising should be banned. To what extent do you agree or disagree?” b) “More people are moving to cities. Why is this happening, and what problems does it create?”
blocks.answer: a) Opinion. Deliver a clear position on banning advertising, defended throughout. b) Two-part (cause and problem). Deliver the causes of urban migration and the problems it creates, both developed.

blocks.label: Drill 23.2 (brainstorming)
blocks.prompt: For “Governments should tax unhealthy food to improve public health. To what extent do you agree?”, pick three relevant lenses and give one idea each.
blocks.answer: Health (reduced disease from lower consumption); Economy (revenue raised, but a burden on poorer households); Individual (freedom of choice versus nudging healthier behaviour). Three relevant lenses; note that Environment or Culture would be a stretch here.

blocks.text: Task 1 drills
Drill 23.3 (overview): For the device-ownership table (from File 17, repeated below), write a number-free overview.

blocks.label: Drill 23.3 (overview)
blocks.prompt: For the device-ownership table above, write a number-free overview.
blocks.answer: “Overall, ownership of most devices rose over the decade, most sharply for smartphones and smart TVs, while desktop computers were the only category to become less common.” Whole picture, the exception named, no numbers.

blocks.label: Drill 23.4 (data selection)
blocks.prompt: From the same table, list the three features worth reporting in the body.
blocks.answer: (1) smartphones rose most (35 to 88); (2) smart TVs rose sharply from a low base (10 to 65); (3) desktop PCs fell, the only decline (60 to 30). Group the two risers, contrast the faller as the exception.

blocks.text: Paragraph drills

blocks.label: Drill 23.5 (development)
blocks.prompt: Develop this bare point using Point, Explanation, Example, Consequence: “Taxing unhealthy food could reduce consumption.”
blocks.answer: “Taxing unhealthy food could reduce how much of it people buy. (Point.) Higher prices tend to discourage consumption, especially of non-essential items, because cost influences everyday choices at the point of sale. (Explanation.) When some countries introduced taxes on sugary drinks, for instance, sales of those drinks noticeably fell. (Example.) Over time, this could shift diets towards healthier options and ease the burden on public health systems. (Consequence.)”

blocks.label: Drill 23.6 (introduction)
blocks.prompt: Paraphrase this prompt for an introduction, without copying it: “Some believe that children should be taught to compete, while others think cooperation is more valuable.”
blocks.answer: “Whether schools should encourage competition or cooperation among children is a subject of ongoing debate.” The prompt's meaning is kept; its wording is changed, so it scores for Lexical Resource rather than being discounted as copying.

blocks.label: Drill 23.7 (conclusion)
blocks.prompt: Write a two-sentence conclusion for an essay that argued cooperation is more valuable than competition, adding no new idea.
blocks.answer: “In conclusion, while competition has its place, the ability to work well with others is the more valuable skill for children to develop. Schools that prioritise cooperation are therefore likely to prepare their pupils better for adult life.” Restates the position, summarises, adds nothing new.

blocks.text: Full-task exercises

blocks.label: Drill 23.8 (full Task 1)
blocks.prompt: Using the device table above, write a full Task 1 answer (introduction, overview, one or two body paragraphs), in about 15 minutes.
blocks.answer: This is a full writing task; assess yours against the criteria. Check: a paraphrased introduction, a clear number-free overview, and body paragraphs that select and group data with a few key figures.

blocks.label: Drill 23.9 (full Task 2)
blocks.prompt: Write a full essay in about 40 minutes: “In many countries, people are working longer hours. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?”
blocks.answer: This is a full writing task; assess yours against the criteria. Check: a clear verdict in the introduction (the word “outweigh” demands one), both sides covered, each idea developed with Point-Explanation-Example-Consequence, and a conclusion confirming which side outweighs, with no new idea.

blocks.label: Drill 23.10 (timed challenge)
blocks.prompt: Do Drills 23.8 and 23.9 back to back in 60 minutes, applying the time plan from File 22.
blocks.answer: The challenge is not just writing both but pacing them: Task 1 capped at twenty minutes, Task 2 given its full forty, with planning and checking inside each. If you overran Task 1, log it and do Task 2 first next time.

blocks.text: BAND COMPARISON: what lifts a paragraph
Same point, two bands. Read both and see the difference.
Band 6 body paragraph: “Firstly, longer hours are bad. Moreover, people get tired. In addition, they have no time for family. Furthermore, this is a big problem. Additionally, health can suffer.”
Why Band 6: the ideas are listed, not developed; every sentence opens with a mechanical linker; nothing is explained or illustrated. It is a chain of assertions.

Band 8 body paragraph: “The most serious drawback of longer working hours is the toll they take on wellbeing. When employees spend more of each day at work, they have less time to rest and to see their families, and chronic tiredness gradually undermines both their health and their relationships. A parent working twelve-hour shifts, for example, may rarely see their children awake, straining family life in ways that no salary fully compensates for. Over time, such pressure can lead to burnout, which harms not only the worker but the employer who loses them.”

Why Band 8: one clear point, explained (why longer hours harm wellbeing), illustrated (the twelve-hour-shift parent), and carried to a consequence (burnout affecting both sides). The cohesion is invisible, through referencing and logic, with no mechanical linkers. The vocabulary is precise and natural, not forced.
The gap between the two is not rare words or complex grammar. It is development, natural cohesion, and precise word choice, exactly the strategies of Files 20 and 21.
MODULE 3 WRAP-UP: WRITING IN ONE BREATH
Compressed to its core, Writing is this:

Read the question twice and identify exactly what it asks, every part of it. For Task 1, read the visual, find the overview, and select and group the data rather than dumping it. For Task 2, take a clear position, generate relevant ideas with the lens menu, and develop two or three of them fully with point, explanation, example, and consequence. Structure flexibly, one job per paragraph, and connect through logic and referencing rather than a pile of linkers. Choose precise, natural words over forced impressive ones. Give Task 2 its full share of the hour, and spend the last minutes checking that you answered the whole question before you check anything else.

That is the whole module. Not “write well,” but a precise sequence of analysing, planning, developing, and checking, that you can now run on any prompt. When you can do it without thinking, the blank page stops being frightening, because you always know what to put on it.
You should now be able to say, of any Task 1 visual and any Task 2 prompt:
“I know exactly what the question is asking and how to build my answer.”
Three modules down. Turn next to Module 4, Speaking, where there is no page to plan on and no time to check, only you, the examiner, and the words as they come.
